transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well… I came in because even on my better days, I can’t quite shake this feeling that some people at church, and in the walking club too, are sort of watching me. Like they’ll put little messages about me in the bulletin, or say things in a way that feels meant for me. I know that probably sounds odd… but it’s been bothering me.
When you notice these messages or comments, are you completely certain they are meant for you?

I wouldn’t say completely certain… I mean, I try to tell myself maybe it’s just a bulletin or just someone making a comment. But then it’ll feel so pointed, like they’re watching me or slipping in little messages about me. At church especially, or sometimes with the walking club.

It’s funny, the church bulletin has always had little announcements, birthdays and bake sale things—my mother used to save every one of those, she had a whole drawer—but now I’ll read something and think, “Why did they put it that way?” Like it’s meant for me, even if I can’t prove it.
Do you believe these messages are definitely intended for you?

Definitely… I don’t know if I’d use that word. It feels very much like they are, like at church or in the walking club, people are watching me and slipping little messages into the bulletin or the way they say things.

But then I think, well, maybe I’m reading too much into it. My neighbor used to say church ladies can make anything sound pointed, you know, especially when they’re organizing events and all that. But still… even on better days, I can’t quite shake the feeling it’s about me.
Have you heard voices when no one else was there?

Sometimes, yes… mostly when the house is real quiet. I’ll hear my name, or just a few words, and it sounds like my friend’s voice coming from the kitchen or sometimes the porch.

It’s clear enough that I’ll answer back before I remember nobody’s there. Then I feel silly, you know. The kitchen carries sound funny anyway—my old refrigerator makes these little clicks, and my mother used to say houses talk at night—but this is more like someone saying something, not just a noise.
During these times, have you had a period when you felt unusually depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

Yes… yes, I have. It’s been most days, really, this deep sadness kind of sitting on me. And guilt too, and not wanting to do much of anything I used to enjoy.

I’d say it’s been going on about… a year and two months now. I remember because I kept thinking it would pass after the seasons changed, you know, but then it was still there.
Have you heard those voices at times when you were not feeling depressed?

Yes… there was a time, a few weeks maybe, where I wasn’t feeling quite so sunk down. I was getting dressed in the mornings, eating a little better, keeping up with things more.

My sister used to say you can tell a person’s state by whether they put on real shoes or just slippers, and I was putting on shoes then. But even during that spell, I still heard my name in the house sometimes. And at church, I still had that feeling people were sort of hinting about me. So it wasn’t only when I was feeling real depressed.
Have the voices and the feeling that people are sending you messages been going on for longer than one month?

Yes… definitely longer than a month. It’s hard to pin it down exactly, because I keep thinking of it by what was going on around the house—like when I moved those boxes in the hall and then never really finished them—but I’d say the voices and the messages feeling… and even getting my thoughts all tangled up… that’s been about eleven months now.
Was there ever a stretch of at least two weeks when you were hearing the voices or feeling people were sending you messages, but you were not depressed?

Yes… yes, I think so. There was that spell for several weeks where I wasn’t so weighed down. I was getting dressed in the morning, eating a bit better… I even remember putting on proper shoes, which sounds silly, but it felt like something.

But the voices didn’t stop. I’d still hear my name in the house sometimes. And at church, I still thought people were kind of hinting about me, like there were messages in what they were saying. So yes, even when I wasn’t feeling so depressed, that was still happening.
Have you ever had a period when you felt unusually high, euphoric, or full of energy?

I’m not sure I’d call it “high,” exactly. I mean, I’ve had days where I got a little more done, like I’d start sorting a drawer and then remember an old receipt from a store that closed years ago—funny how those things stick with you.

But unusually euphoric or full of energy… I don’t really know. I don’t think so, not in the way you’re asking. Could you say what you mean by unusually?
Have you found yourself speaking much less than you used to?

Yes… I think I do talk less. Like at coffee hour, I used to at least make a little conversation, ask about someone’s grandkids or the bake sale—though the muffins they had last time were too dry, I remember thinking that.

But now I mostly just sit there. Even if someone tells a funny story, I don’t really laugh or say much. My face just stays kind of flat, like the feeling is in there somewhere but it doesn’t come out.
Did these experiences begin after you had a medical illness, head injury, seizure, or started a new medicine?

I don’t… I don’t think I can point to something like that. Not like, “oh, after that one illness” or after bumping my head or anything clear.

I mean, I’ve had ordinary things over the years, colds and aches and all that—at my age you start keeping track of appointments on little scraps of paper, and then you can never find the right one. But I can’t say this started right after something medical or a new pill. It just sort of… came on, as far as I remember.
Since these experiences began, has it become much harder for you to manage your usual daily activities?

Yes… it has, I suppose. I still live at home, so it’s not like I can’t do anything for myself, but I don’t keep up with things like I used to.

I stopped going to the quilting gatherings mostly. I used to like seeing what fabrics people picked—there was one lady who always used these bright yellows, even in winter, which I thought was funny. And the walking club too… I just don’t really go now. The garden has gotten away from me some as well.

My daughter’s been checking in more, making sure I’ve eaten and that I remember appointments. I don’t like needing that, but… yes, daily things are harder than before.
Have you had any episodes of confusion or memory trouble around the time these experiences started?

I’m not sure… not in a big obvious way, I don’t think. I mean, I forget little things sometimes—where I set my glasses, or I’ll go into the pantry and then wonder what I went in for. But my sister says everybody does that, and she once put the milk in the cupboard, so… 

Around when all this started, I can’t remember there being some spell where I was confused, like not knowing where I was or anything. It’s more… hard to say. Time kind of blurs together when you’re not doing much.
Have you been having trouble with your memory lately?

Lately… I don’t know if I’d call it real trouble. I misplace things, sure—my reading glasses, mostly, and once I found them on top of the washing machine, which makes no sense because I wasn’t doing laundry. Or I’ll stand there with the refrigerator open and forget what I wanted.

But then my neighbor does that too, and she’s sharp as a tack—she still remembers everyone’s birthdays, even the mailman’s children. So… I’m not sure. Nothing that feels like I’m losing whole chunks, if that’s what you mean. Just little forgetful things.
Have you been having more trouble finding the right words when you speak?

More trouble finding words… I don’t think so, not especially. I mean, sometimes I’ll forget the name of a thing, like that little metal… oh, the bobbin, for the sewing machine. But that’s been happening to people my age forever, hasn’t it?

My sister used to say “the thingamajig” for everything, even when she was in her forties, and we all knew what she meant. So I don’t know if mine is any worse. I haven’t really noticed myself getting stuck in conversations, no.
Have other people told you that your speech is hard to follow or seems jumbled?

Sometimes, yes. My daughter will say, “Mom, I’m not following you,” and I think I was making sense when I started. Like I’ll be trying to explain something about the mail, or what someone said after church, and then somehow I’m talking about quilt patterns and the birds outside and… warnings I thought were important.

And then I look at their faces and they’ve got that polite look, like they don’t know where I landed. I don’t mean to do it. In my head it feels connected, but I guess it comes out all tangled.
During the months since these problems began, has your depression been present for most of that time?

Yes… I think so. It hasn’t been every single minute, but most of these months, that low feeling has been there, like a gray sweater I can’t take off. The guilt too—over little things, old things. And I haven’t wanted to do much, even things I used to like.

There were times when the other… worries, or noises, seemed quieter, and I’d think maybe I should feel better then. But the sadness was still kind of sitting in the room with me.
Have you been seeing things that other people don’t seem to see?

Seeing things? No, not really seeing, I don’t think. Not like a person standing there.

It’s more… sometimes when the house is real quiet, I’ll hear my name, or just a few words, and it sounds like my friend’s voice from the kitchen, or out by the porch. Clear enough that I’ll answer back, you know—like “What?”—and then I remember nobody’s there. The kitchen does carry sound funny, though. My old neighbor used to say pipes can make a house talk, and I suppose old houses do have their ways… but no, seeing things, I don’t think so.
Has a doctor told you that you have dementia or Alzheimer’s disease?

No… I don’t think any doctor has told me that. Not Alzheimer’s. I mean, they’ve asked me questions before, little memory-type questions, and I always get nervous because when someone puts you on the spot, suddenly even the day of the week feels like it’s hiding under the table.

But no, nobody has said dementia or Alzheimer’s to me that I remember. My aunt had people worried about that when she got older, and everyone started labeling her forgetful even when she just misplaced her glasses, so… I try not to jump to those words.

doctor.question: Have other people told you that your speech is hard to follow or seems jumbled?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
target_item.manifestation: When I try to explain things, I start with one thought about the mail or church and end up talking about quilt patterns, birds, and warnings, and then I can see people don't know what I'm getting at.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether others have noticed the patient's speech is hard to follow or jumbled, which directly matches disorganized thinking or speech.

patient.answer:
Sometimes, yes. My daughter will say, “Mom, I’m not following you,” and I think I was making sense when I started. Like I’ll be trying to explain something about the mail, or what someone said after church, and then somehow I’m talking about quilt patterns and the birds outside and… warnings I thought were important.

And then I look at their faces and they’ve got that polite look, like they don’t know where I landed. I don’t mean to do it. In my head it feels connected, but I guess it comes out all tangled.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether prominent mood episodes have been present for most of the total duration of the illness, to distinguish schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia.
doctor.question: During the months since these problems began, has your depression been present for most of that time?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: For most of this whole stretch, the sadness, guilt, and loss of interest have been there in the background, even during times when the voices or suspicious thoughts were quieter.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether depression has been present for most of the time since the problems began, which directly matches this duration/majority criterion.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. It hasn’t been every single minute, but most of these months, that low feeling has been there, like a gray sweater I can’t take off. The guilt too—over little things, old things. And I haven’t wanted to do much, even things I used to like.

There were times when the other… worries, or noises, seemed quieter, and I’d think maybe I should feel better then. But the sadness was still kind of sitting in the room with me.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is an underlying medical cause for the psychosis by screening for visual hallucinations, which would raise concern for an organic etiology such as F06.2 over primary schizophrenia-spectrum disorders.
doctor.question: Have you been seeing things that other people don’t seem to see?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes when the house is quiet I hear my name or a few words in my friend's voice from the kitchen or porch, clear enough that I answer before I remember nobody is there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about perceiving things others do not see, which is a hallucination-related symptom.

patient.answer:
Seeing things? No, not really seeing, I don’t think. Not like a person standing there.

It’s more… sometimes when the house is real quiet, I’ll hear my name, or just a few words, and it sounds like my friend’s voice from the kitchen, or out by the porch. Clear enough that I’ll answer back, you know—like “What?”—and then I remember nobody’s there. The kitchen does carry sound funny, though. My old neighbor used to say pipes can make a house talk, and I suppose old houses do have their ways… but no, seeing things, I don’t think so.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is evidence of an underlying medical or neurological cause for the psychosis, which would help distinguish organic delusional disorder from primary schizophrenia-spectrum illness.
doctor.question: Has a doctor told you that you have dementia or Alzheimer’s disease?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether the patient has been diagnosed with dementia or Alzheimer’s disease, which is not covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
No… I don’t think any doctor has told me that. Not Alzheimer’s. I mean, they’ve asked me questions before, little memory-type questions, and I always get nervous because when someone puts you on the spot, suddenly even the day of the week feels like it’s hiding under the table.

But no, nobody has said dementia or Alzheimer’s to me that I remember. My aunt had people worried about that when she got older, and everyone started labeling her forgetful even when she just misplaced her glasses, so… I try not to jump to those words.

opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has persistent psychotic symptoms for about 11 months, including auditory hallucinations, referential/persecutory ideas, disorganized/tangled thought/speech, and negative symptoms. She also has a major depressive syndrome present for most of the illness duration (about 14 months, most months depressed with guilt and anhedonia). Crucially, psychotic symptoms persisted for several weeks, including at least 2 weeks, during a period when she was not depressed, supporting schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, rather than psychotic depression. The prominence of mood symptoms for the majority of the total illness favors F25.1 over schizophrenia. No clear medical/neurologic trigger, delirium, dementia, or medication cause was established, arguing against F06.2.
